title: Whole-mount immunostaining protocol for eastern subterranean termite brains
author: Merchant, Zhou
materials: Brains are washed in PBST to clean them of leftover reagents, then incubated in the secondary antibody, which binds to the primary antibody and possesses a fluorescent tag.8.Wash brains in PBST three times for 15 min each.9.Incubate brains in 100 μL secondary antibody, Alexa Fluor 546 goat anti-mouse IgG, at 1:500 at 4°C for 18–24 h.a.Mix 95 μL PBST with 5 μL NGS and 0.2 μL Alexa Fluor 546 goat anti-mouse IgG.Note: If using additional secondary antibodies and co-staining, they should be included in this step. Take care to ensure that fluorescence spectra do not overlap. There are many online resources that can be used to check for spectra overlap when designing experiments, for example https://www.thermofisher.com/order/fluorescence-spectraviewer/.

steps.title: Prepare poly‑L‑lysine coating solution
steps.instruction: Make a poly‑L‑lysine (PLL) solution for coverslip adhesion and store it at 4 °C in darkness.

substeps.instruction: Allow PLL powder to reach room temperature (≈20‑25 °C).
Add 2 mL ultrapure water to the original container, mix until dissolved.
Transfer the mixture to a 50 mL conical tube.
Add 30 mL ultrapure water to the tube, mix thoroughly.
Add 64 µL Kodak Photo‑Flo 200 solution, mix thoroughly.
Transfer the final solution to a glass coverslip jar until the jar is almost full.
Store both the coverslip jar and the remaining solution in the conical tube at 4 °C in total darkness (usable up to 12 months; reuse the jar solution as needed).

steps.title: Anesthetize termites on ice
steps.instruction: Place termites in a microcentrifuge tube (or similar container) and submerge in ice for more than 2 min until they cease moving.

steps.title: Dissect brains in PBS
steps.instruction: Under a dissecting microscope, remove the head, cut away cuticle, expose the brain, and gently free it from surrounding tissue while keeping the subesophageal zone intact if desired.

substeps.instruction: Perform dissection in a dish containing phosphate‑buffered saline (PBS).
Use one pair of forceps to grip the posterior end of the head; use the other pair to cut the cuticle along the sides and top.
Remove translucent muscle and any white fibrous tracheal strings attached to the brain, taking care not to damage the brain.

steps.title: Transfer brains to ice‑cold PBS tube
steps.instruction: Collect each dissected brain with the sides of the forceps (do not grasp the brain) and place it into a 2 mL microcentrifuge tube containing PBS kept on ice.

substeps.instruction: Brains can remain in ice‑cold PBS for 3–4 h without major loss of quality; shorter times are preferable.

steps.title: Fix brains with 2 % PFA
steps.instruction: Replace PBS with 1.5 mL 2 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) and fix brains for 55 min while nutating at 100–120 RPM.

substeps.instruction: Use a pipette to remove as much PBS as possible without aspirating brains (a 1000 µL pipette is adequate; for volumes <200 µL use a 200 µL or smaller pipette).
Place the tube on an orbital shaker set to approximately 100–120 RPM for the entire fixation period.

steps.title: Wash brains in 10 % PBST
steps.instruction: Wash brains three times with 10 % PBST, 15 min per wash, nutating at 100–120 RPM.

steps.title: Block with 5 % normal goat serum
steps.instruction: Incubate brains in 100 µL of 5 % normal goat serum (NGS) for 1 h at room temperature while nutating.

substeps.instruction: Prepare blocking solution by mixing 95 µL PBST with 5 µL NGS.

steps.title: Incubate with primary anti‑nc82 antibody
steps.instruction: Incubate brains in 102 µL of primary antibody (mouse anti‑nc82, 1:50) at 4 °C for 18–24 h while nutating.

substeps.instruction: Prepare primary mix: 95 µL PBST + 5 µL NGS + 2 µL mouse anti‑nc82.
If co‑staining, add additional primary antibodies (not derived from mouse or goat) to the same mix.

steps.title: Wash brains after primary incubation
steps.instruction: Wash brains three times with PBST, 15 min each, nutating at 100–120 RPM.

steps.title: Incubate with Alexa Fluor 546 secondary antibody
steps.instruction: Incubate brains in 100 µL of secondary antibody (Alexa Fluor 546 goat anti‑mouse IgG, 1:500) at 4 °C for 18–24 h while nutating.

substeps.instruction: Prepare secondary mix: 95 µL PBST + 5 µL NGS + 0.2 µL Alexa Fluor 546 goat anti‑mouse IgG.
If co‑staining, add any additional secondary antibodies ensuring non‑overlapping fluorescence spectra.

description: The brain plays a vital role in controlling insect behavior, yet despite this importance remains poorly understood beyond a basic organizational level in many non-model organisms.2 Immunostaining is a commonly applied technique in model insects such as Drosophila that can be used to visualize the entire brain as well as specific populations of neurons.3,4,5 During immunostaining, brain tissue is incubated in a primary antibody that binds to a protein of interest. Tissue is then commonly incubated in a secondary antibody, which binds to the primary antibody and possesses a tag that can be visualized using confocal or epifluorescence microscopy.6 Termites, despite their ecological dominance and economic significance,7 are one such non-model insect for which, until recently, little information existed regarding the brain. In our study, we imaged the brains of individuals from different castes of one of the most widely distributed termite species in the world, the eastern subterranean termite, Reticulitermes flavipes, and compared differences in brain allometry between castes.1 To do this, we adapted a whole mount immunostaining protocol from Drosophila, which possesses a brain similar in size to that of R. flavipes, that uses the commercially available antibody nc82.3 nc82 targets the protein Bruchpilot, which is expressed at presynaptic active zones.8 In theory, co-staining with other antibodies should also be possible to visualize protein expression patterns within the brain, although we have not directly tested this because for our study we focused on the structure of the brain itself rather than specific proteins. Further adaptation of this protocol to other non-model insects may also be useful as it is relatively inexpensive to perform and is fairly simple except for the dissection and mounting steps, which are likely to require some level of trial and error before producing satisfactory results.
